All confirmed. Here is the incident report.

---

# Incident Report: STRRAT RAT Infection

**Evidence reviewed:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 frames, 585.7s duration). No IDS/alert exports or other artifacts were present in the evidence directory — the pcap was the only file.

## Victim Host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **172.16.1.66** | Consistent local source of all suspicious traffic |
| MAC address | **00:1e:64:ec:f3:08** | ARP: `arp.src.proto_ipv4==172.16.1.66` bound to this MAC; matches `eth.src` on all frames from 172.16.1.66 |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-SKBR25F** | NBNS name registration from 172.16.1.66 (`DESKTOP-SKBR25F<00>`); confirmed again inside the STRRAT beacon payload itself |
| Logged-in user | **ccollier** (Clark Collier) | Kerberos `CNameString` = `ccollier` on AS-REQ/TGS traffic between 172.16.1.66 and the DC (172.16.1.4); LDAP resolves the account to `CN=Clark Collier,CN=Users,DC=wiresharkworkshop,DC=online`; same username appears inside the STRRAT beacon payload |

Domain: `wiresharkworkshop.online`, domain controller `WIRESHARK-WS-DC` at 172.16.1.4 (MAC `5c:f9:dd:8c:97:35`). All AD traffic (LDAP, Kerberos, DCERPC/DRSUAPI, SMB2) is between the victim and this DC and is normal domain-join background activity, not malicious.

## Malware Family

**STRRAT** (Java-based remote access trojan). **Attribution: signature-confirmed** — the C2 heartbeat protocol literally names the malware in cleartext on the wire.

At frame 9066 (t=76.99s), 172.16.1.66 opens a raw TCP connection to `141.98.10.79:12132` (no TLS handshake, no DNS lookup preceding it — the IP appears hardcoded in the malware's config). Following TCP stream 83 shows a plaintext pipe-delimited beacon repeating every ~5 seconds for the rest of the capture (last beacon at t=585.66s, connection still open when the capture ends, no FIN/RST observed):

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender||1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|<uptime>
```

Field breakdown: literal malware name `STRRAT`, campaign/build ID `1BE8292C`, victim hostname, victim username, OS, architecture, installed AV (Windows Defender), STRRAT client version `1.6`, victim country, ransomware-module install status (`Not Installed`), and infection uptime counter. This matches STRRAT's documented client fingerprint/check-in format exactly.

One second after the C2 connection opened, the host also issued a plaintext HTTP request to `ip-api.com` (`GET /json/`, spoofed `Chrome/73.0.3683.86` User-Agent) which returned the victim's public-IP geolocation (Austin, TX / Google Fiber). This is a self-fingerprinting lookup, consistent with STRRAT's startup behavior and matching the "US:United States" field sent in the beacon — not attacker infrastructure itself, but it's tightly time-correlated with the C2 connection and corroborates the beacon.

No SMTP/POP/IMAP/FTP traffic exists in this capture, and the only plaintext HTTP requests are the Windows connectivity check, the ip-api.com lookup, and SSDP M-SEARCH broadcasts — so the initial delivery vector (malspam attachment, drive-by download, etc.) is **not observable in this capture**; the pcap begins with the infection already resident and the RAT initiating its first C2 connection.

## Indicators of Compromise

```json
{
  "victim": {
    "ip": "172.16.1.66",
    "mac": "00:1e:64:ec:f3:08",
    "hostname": "DESKTOP-SKBR25F",
    "user": "ccollier"
  },
  "malware_family": "STRRAT",
  "attribution_confidence": "signature-confirmed",
  "iocs": [
    {
      "type": "c2_endpoint",
      "value": "141.98.10.79:12132",
      "evidence": "TCP stream 83, frames 9066-11562: persistent plaintext connection, no DNS lookup preceding it, repeated ~5s pipe-delimited beacon self-identifying as 'ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|...'; connection still open at end of capture"
    }
  ],
  "benign_context": [
    {"item": "ip-api.com (208.95.112.1:80)", "note": "GET /json/ geolocation self-lookup, frame 9111 / TCP stream 84, time-correlated with C2 connect but a public IP-geolocation service, not attacker infrastructure"},
    {"item": "repo1.maven.org (199.232.196.209)", "note": "8.8 MB TLS download ending just before the C2 connection opens; SNI-confirmed as the legitimate Maven Central CDN, no plaintext content observable to prove or disprove a relationship to the infection"},
    {"item": "Microsoft/Windows telemetry and O365 domains", "note": "config.edge.skype.com, mobile.events.data.microsoft.com, login.microsoftonline.com, officeapps.live.com, msn.com/bing.com family, github.com/objects.githubusercontent.com, javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com — all standard Windows 11/Office/dev-tool background traffic"},
    {"item": "172.16.1.4 (WIRESHARK-WS-DC)", "note": "domain controller; all LDAP/Kerberos/SMB2/DCERPC traffic to it is normal AD authentication, not malicious"}
  ],
  "incident_summary": "Windows 11 workstation DESKTOP-SKBR25F (172.16.1.66, MAC 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08), logged in as domain user ccollier, is infected with the STRRAT Java-based RAT. The malware opened a persistent raw-TCP C2 channel to 141.98.10.79:12132 and beaconed a self-identifying plaintext ping every ~5 seconds for the remainder of the capture, disclosing hostname, username, OS, and AV product to the operator. The infection vector is not present in this capture; the pcap captures only the ongoing C2 session, not the initial compromise."
}
```

No file transfers, downloaded executables, or exportable objects tied to the infection were observed in the capture (`--export-objects http` yields only the Windows connectivity-check response and the JSON geolocation reply — neither is a malicious payload), so no file name or SHA256 hash can be grounded in the evidence.

**Recommended action:** isolate DESKTOP-SKBR25F (172.16.1.66) from the network immediately, block outbound traffic to 141.98.10.79:12132 at the perimeter, force a password reset for the `ccollier` domain account, and image the host for offline forensic analysis to recover the STRRAT jar and determine the delivery vector, since it is not visible in this capture.
